newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Hang Seng seen to gain from handover.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Hang Seng seen to gain from handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule should boost Hong Kong stocks both before and after the handover, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

An average of six forecasts collected last week from Hong Kong-based equity analysts predicted the Hang Seng Index would end 1997 at around just under 15,000 points, an increase of some 14 percent from the March 12 close of 13,119.13.

Hong Kong stocks have consolidated in a range of 13,000-13,800, but equity analysts expect the market to have another run at its record high before the British colony returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30. The Hang Seng hit an all-time closing high of 13,868.24 on January 20 this year.
They predicted more funds would flow into Hong Kong from China as Chinese macroeconomic controls were relaxed.

Analysts said Hong Kong stocks would continue to climb in 1998, boosted by continued economic growth in China, a reasonably strong U.S. economy and core countries in Europe emerging from their economic slowdown.
An average of five forecasts showed the Hang Seng Index soaring by 35 percent to around 17,800 by the end of next year.
The only dampening factor for stocks was the possibility of monetary tightening or increasing regulation if the Hong Kong and Chinese economies overheated.
BEN KWONG, DIRECTOR OF RESEARCH, DHARMALA SECURITIES.

"I think it is mainly because of the quite widely expected smooth transition and also some specific 1997 factors. China is going to further relax macroeconomic controls, we will see more Chinese funds flowing into Hong Kong - like the property sector and the equity market as well - so the index may overshoot a bit."

"Asset prices have moved up quite nicely and in 1998 we may see some unfavourable figures that will affect market sentiment like the interest rate trend and also probably a little bit of overheating of the Hong Kong and Chinese economies. That will lead to some sort of regulation or may be some sort of tightening so that will have a negative impact."
PETER CHURCHOUSE, REGIONAL STRATEGIST, MORGAN STANLEY.

"Last year the market traded through most of the middle of the year in a very tight range and as you saw evidence of the property market kicking in and the realisation that the U.S. had not jacked up interest rates, the market took off again. I think we will probably see a similar pattern this year."
